author: hlntnr
text:
Can ML systems "think"? Are they "intelligent"? I honestly don't care. What matters is what capabilities & weaknesses they have, how we use them in practice, and what harms/benefits result. 

Definitional debates about what "real" intelligence is rarely help answer those Qs.
3/3

author: hlntnr
text:
The point isn't "what a dumb comparison, swimming is so much more than what submarines do." 

The point is that our everyday words often bunch together multiple different concepts, and when we encounter something new (like submarines or AI), we need to disentangle & unpack. 
2/3

author: hlntnr
text:
One of my favorite quotes on AI is from Dijkstra: 
"The question of whether a computer can think is no more interesting than the question of whether a submarine can swim."

But not just as a clever comeback! 1/3

quoted.text: Debating whether today's AI tools are truly intelligent is about as useful as debating whether a drone is a bird. If you define a bird to be anything of a certain size that flies, then sure. But it's also obvious that drones can't do most of the other things that birds can do.

author: hlntnr
text:
Or in interpretability, it was neat to see a whole cluster about how to convert neural network outputs into decision rules - not an area I'd heard a ton about. And some clusters that we ultimately excluded were super interesting too - e.g. on "disentangled representations."

4/10

author: hlntnr
text:
3 research clusters in robustness, 2 in interpretability, and 3 in reward learning. 

I found it fascinating to see the distribution of topics in different areas, e.g. I knew adversarial examples were a hot topic, but not that they'd be *so* dominant within robustness. 3/10 https://t.co/hxCNxZQ8vN

author: hlntnr
text:
The hardest part was figuring out how to scope "AI safety." In the end we went with 3 categories: robustness, interpretability, and reward learning.

We used keywords to look for plausible clusters in each category, found 42, then checked each one and ended up with 8:

author: hlntnr
text: This piece introduces privacy enhancing technologies (PETs) and lays out the steps we need to take to realize the benefits they could bring. All credit to my coauthors - @Andrew_Imbrie, @danbbaer, @iamtrask, @AnnaPuglisi838, @ErikBrattberg! 2/2

author: hlntnr
text:
A huge misconception that's woven through debates on privacy & tech is that to solve problems with data, you have to compromise privacy. 

This is getting less and less true via the devt of new techs—but democracies need to ensure these are deployed openly & responsibly. 1/2
